# An In-Depth Review of *Middlemarch* by George Eliot

## "The History of Man's Condition": A Comprehensive Critical Study of George Eliot's Masterwork

---

## Preface: Why *Middlemarch* Demands Our Sustained Attention

There is a particular kind of novel that does not merely tell a story but constructs a world so complete, so morally intricate, and so psychologically penetrating that the reader emerges from it genuinely altered — not in the dramatic, thunderclap fashion of a conversion experience, but in the slower, more durable way that comes from having spent extended time in the company of a profoundly intelligent mind. George Eliot's *Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life*, published in eight installments between 1871 and 1872, is precisely such a novel. Virginia Woolf, not a writer given to easy superlatives, called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." Henry James, whose own novelistic ambitions were shaped in part by his encounter with Eliot's work, recognized in it a seriousness of moral and artistic purpose that he spent his career attempting to match. More than a century and a half after its publication, *Middlemarch* continues to reward — indeed, to demand — the kind of sustained, attentive reading that its author brought to the writing of it.

This review aims to do justice to that demand. It will examine the novel's historical and biographical context, its structural architecture, its major themes (including the nature of idealism, the politics of marriage, the relationship between the individual and society, the problem of egoism, and the possibility of moral progress), its narrative technique and prose style, its characterization, and its lasting significance. The goal is not merely to summarize or to praise, but to think alongside the novel — to take seriously its invitation to examine the conditions under which human beings live, fail, and occasionally, quietly, do good.

---

## Part One: Context and Genesis

### George Eliot and the Making of *Middlemarch*

To understand *Middlemarch*, one must understand something of the woman who wrote it, because the novel is, among other things, a sustained meditation on the relationship between intellectual ambition and social constraint — a relationship that Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), who published under the male pseudonym George Eliot, knew with an intimacy that was both personal and painful.

Evans was born in Warwickshire, the daughter of a land agent, and received an unusually thorough education for a woman of her time and class. She read voraciously, taught herself German, French, Italian, Latin, and Greek, and by her mid-twenties had translated David Friedrich Strauss's *Das Leben Jesu* (1846) and Ludwig Feuerbach's *Das Wesen des Christenthums* (1854) — works of German biblical criticism and humanist philosophy that had profound effects on her thinking. The translation of Strauss in particular was an act of intellectual courage: the book argued that the Gospels were mythological rather than historical documents, and its publication in English was considered scandalous. Evans had already, by this point, lost her Christian faith, a loss that caused a painful rupture with her father and that she would spend the rest of her life processing — not by returning to orthodoxy, but by developing what we might call a secular religion of human sympathy and moral seriousness.

Her relationship with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes, which began in 1854 and lasted until his death in 1878, was the central emotional fact of her adult life. Because Lewes was legally married to another woman (though separated), their union could not be formalized, and Evans was consequently ostracized from polite society. She and Lewes lived together openly, she referring to him as her husband, and the social consequences were severe: many of her former acquaintances refused to receive her, and she was excluded from the respectable drawing rooms of Victorian England. This experience of social marginalization — of being a person of exceptional intelligence and moral seriousness who was nonetheless judged and condemned by the very society she sought to understand — is everywhere present in *Middlemarch*, most obviously in the figure of Dorothea Brooke, but also in the fates of Lydgate, Bulstrode, and Casaubon.

Evans did not begin writing fiction until she was nearly forty, encouraged by Lewes, who recognized her gifts and provided the emotional and practical support that made her career possible. Her early novels — *Adam Bede* (1859), *The Mill on the Floss* (1860), *Silas Marner* (1861) — established her reputation as one of the foremost novelists of her age. *Middlemarch* was her sixth novel, begun in 1869 and completed in 1872, and it represents the fullest expression of her novelistic powers.

The novel originated as two separate projects. The first was a story about Dorothea Brooke, a young woman of idealistic temperament who makes a disastrous marriage to an elderly scholar. The second was a story about Tertius Lydgate, an ambitious young doctor who comes to the provincial town of Middlemarch with plans to reform medical practice and conduct important scientific research. Eliot eventually recognized that these two stories belonged together — that they were, in fact, variations on the same theme — and wove them into the vast, intricate tapestry that is *Middlemarch*.

### The Historical Setting

The novel is set in the years 1829–1832, a period of intense political and social ferment in England. The Reform Act of 1832, which extended the franchise and redistributed parliamentary seats, was the defining political event of the era, and its approach provides the novel's political backdrop. The period also saw the beginnings of the railway age, the professionalization of medicine, and the early stirrings of what would become the Victorian crisis of faith. Eliot sets her novel in this moment of transition deliberately: Middlemarch is a society on the cusp of change, and her characters are people who must navigate between the old world and the new.

The choice of a provincial setting is equally deliberate. Middlemarch is not London; it is not the center of power or fashion or intellectual life. It is a middling English town — the name itself suggests mediocrity, the middle of things — and its inhabitants are, for the most part, middling people: not great heroes or villains, but ordinary men and women trying to live their lives with some degree of dignity and purpose. This is precisely Eliot's point. The great dramas of human life — the struggles between idealism and compromise, between love and self-interest, between moral aspiration and social constraint — are not confined to the courts of kings or the salons of the great. They play out, every day, in the drawing rooms and consulting rooms and counting houses of places like Middlemarch.

---

## Part Two: Structure and Architecture

### The Novel as Web

*Middlemarch* is a long novel — approximately 900 pages in most modern editions — and its length is not accidental. Eliot needs the space she takes because she is attempting something genuinely ambitious: to render the full complexity of a social world, to show how individual lives are shaped by and in turn shape the communities in which they are embedded. The novel's famous metaphor for its own structure is the web: "I at least have so much to do in unraveling certain human lots, and seeing how they were woven and interwoven, that all the light I can command must be concentrated on this particular web, and not dispersed over that tempting range of relevancies called the universe."

The web metaphor is apt in multiple ways. First, it suggests interconnection: the characters in *Middlemarch* are not isolated individuals but nodes in a network of relationships, obligations, and mutual dependencies. What Lydgate does affects Bulstrode; what Bulstrode does affects Lydgate; what Lydgate does affects Rosamond; what Rosamond does affects Lydgate and Dorothea and Will Ladislaw and, ultimately, the entire community. The novel traces these connections with extraordinary care, showing how actions ripple outward in ways their agents cannot foresee.

Second, the web metaphor suggests fragility and entrapment. Webs catch things; they hold things in place; they can be beautiful and they can be deadly. Many of the novel's characters find themselves caught in webs of their own making — Lydgate in his marriage to Rosamond, Bulstrode in his past, Casaubon in his scholarly project — and the novel is deeply interested in the question of how people become trapped and whether they can free themselves.

Third, the web metaphor suggests the work of making — the patient, painstaking labor of construction. *Middlemarch* is a made thing, and Eliot wants us to be aware of its making. The narrator's presence is constant and conspicuous; we are never allowed to forget that we are reading a novel, that the world we are inhabiting has been constructed by an intelligence that is shaping our perceptions and guiding our sympathies.

### The Four Plots

The novel contains four main narrative strands, each of which is a study in a different kind of idealism and its encounter with reality.

**The Dorothea-Casaubon-Ladislaw plot** is the novel's central strand and the one that most directly engages with the question of female aspiration. Dorothea Brooke is a young woman of exceptional intelligence, moral seriousness, and passionate idealism who longs to do something great with her life. She marries the elderly scholar Edward Casaubon in the belief that she will be his intellectual partner and that his great work — a "Key to All Mythologies" — will give her life meaning and purpose. The marriage is a disaster: Casaubon is cold, jealous, and intellectually sterile, and his great work turns out to be a monument to scholarly futility. After Casaubon's death, Dorothea falls in love with Will Ladislaw, Casaubon's young cousin, and eventually marries him — a choice that, by the terms of Casaubon's will, costs her her fortune.

**The Lydgate-Rosamond plot** is in many ways the novel's most tragic strand. Tertius Lydgate is a brilliant young doctor who comes to Middlemarch with genuine scientific ambitions — he wants to discover the "primitive tissue" that underlies all organic life — and genuine ideals about medical reform. He makes the fatal mistake of marrying Rosamond Vincy, a beautiful, accomplished, and utterly self-absorbed young woman who has no interest in his ambitions and every interest in the social position and material comfort she believes he can provide. The marriage destroys Lydgate: he ends up abandoning his research, going into debt, becoming entangled in Bulstrode's scandal, and eventually practicing fashionable medicine for wealthy patients — a fate he regards as a failure.

**The Bulstrode plot** is the novel's darkest strand, a study in religious hypocrisy and the way the past catches up with us. Nicholas Bulstrode is a wealthy banker and prominent Nonconformist who has built his fortune and his reputation on a foundation of concealed crime. His past eventually catches up with him in the form of John Raffles, a blackmailer who knows his secrets, and the novel traces the terrible logic by which Bulstrode's attempts to protect himself lead him to a moral catastrophe that destroys his reputation and his marriage.

**The Fred Vincy-Mary Garth plot** is the novel's most comic and most hopeful strand. Fred Vincy, Rosamond's brother, is a charming, feckless young man who is in love with Mary Garth, the sensible, clear-eyed daughter of the estate manager Caleb Garth. Mary refuses to marry Fred until he has proved himself capable of honest work, and the plot traces Fred's gradual moral education and his eventual achievement of a modest but genuine happiness.

These four plots are interwoven with extraordinary skill. They share characters, settings, and themes; they illuminate each other by contrast and comparison; and they converge at key moments — most notably in the crisis surrounding Bulstrode's exposure, which brings Lydgate, Dorothea, Will, and the Garths all into contact with each other in ways that test their characters and determine their fates.

### The Prelude and Finale

The novel is framed by a Prelude and a Finale that are among the most important passages in Victorian fiction. The Prelude invokes the figure of Saint Theresa of Ávila, who "found her epos in the reform of a religious order," and asks what becomes of women like Theresa who are born into a world that offers them no such outlet for their "unhistoric acts":

> "Here and there is born a Saint Theresa, foundress of nothing, whose loving heart-beats and sobs after an unattained goodness tremble off and are dispersed among hindrances, instead of centering in some long-recognizable deed."

This passage sets up the novel's central question: what happens to exceptional women in a society that has no place for their exceptionalism? And it frames Dorothea's story not as a personal failure but as a social tragedy — the tragedy of a society that wastes its best human material.

The Finale returns to this question and offers Eliot's most famous and most debated answer:

> "Her finely touched spirit had still its fine issues, though they were not widely visible. Her full nature... spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth. But the effect of her action on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs."

This passage has been read as both consolation and condemnation — as Eliot's affirmation of the value of small, private goodness, and as her indictment of a society that forces its best people into smallness. Both readings are correct, and the tension between them is one of the things that makes *Middlemarch* inexhaustible.

---

## Part Three: Major Themes

### Theme One: The Nature of Idealism and Its Discontents

*Middlemarch* is, at its heart, a novel about idealism — about the human capacity to imagine a better self, a better life, a better world, and about the forces, both internal and external, that frustrate that capacity. Every major character in the novel is, in some sense, an idealist, and every major plot is a study in what happens when idealism meets reality.

Dorothea's idealism is the most conspicuous and the most fully analyzed. She is introduced to us as a young woman who "had a nature altogether ardent, theoretic, and intellectually consequent," who "was enamoured of intensity and greatness, and rash in embracing whatever seemed to her to have those aspects." Her idealism is genuine and admirable, but it is also, as Eliot shows us with characteristic precision, a form of egoism. Dorothea does not see Casaubon as he is; she sees him as she needs him to be — as a great scholar, a Milton, a Pascal, a man whose work will give her life meaning. Her idealism is, in part, a projection of her own needs and desires onto an inadequate object.

This is one of Eliot's most important and most uncomfortable insights: that idealism and egoism are not opposites but are often deeply intertwined. The idealist who wants to do great things, to be part of something larger than herself, is also a person who wants her life to have significance — who wants, in some sense, to be great. Dorothea's desire to serve Casaubon's work is also a desire to participate in greatness, to escape the smallness of ordinary female life. When she discovers that Casaubon's work is futile, she is not only disappointed for him; she is devastated for herself.

Lydgate's idealism is more straightforwardly intellectual. He wants to make a genuine scientific discovery, to reform medical practice, to be a great doctor. His idealism is admirable and, unlike Casaubon's, not futile — he has real talent and real ideas. But his idealism is also accompanied by a blind spot that Eliot diagnoses with devastating precision: "He had not much compass of imagination in regard to the feelings of women." Lydgate can imagine the structure of organic tissue; he cannot imagine the inner life of Rosamond Vincy. He marries her because she is beautiful and because he is attracted to her, without ever seriously considering what kind of person she is or what kind of marriage they will have. His idealism about science coexists with a profound failure of imagination about human beings — specifically, about women.

Casaubon's idealism is the novel's most tragic case, because it is an idealism that has already, by the time we meet him, curdled into something else. He has spent his life on a scholarly project that he knows, at some level, is already obsolete — German scholars have done the work he is attempting, and done it better. His idealism has become a defense mechanism, a way of protecting himself from the knowledge of his own failure. His jealousy of Ladislaw, his cruelty to Dorothea, his obsessive concern with his posthumous reputation — all of these are symptoms of a man who has sacrificed his capacity for genuine human connection on the altar of an ideal that has betrayed him.

Bulstrode's idealism is the most sinister, because it is an idealism that has been used to justify wrongdoing.
